intro: Rachmaninoff’s Barcarolle in G minor, Op. 10 No. 3, marked Moderato, dates from 1894; the melody is in the left hand, below a rocking figure in the right. The composer plays it in his 1919 Edison recording.

sections.label: A · Left-hand melody, Moderato
sections.mNote: Moderato; low melody beneath rocking right-hand thirds

sections.label: B · Semiquavers and held chords, ppp
A′ · Low melody again, Allegro moderato
sections.mNote: Allegro moderato; left-hand melody beneath faster decoration

sections.label: A″ · Slower figures over held chords
sections.mNote: Meno mosso; the right hand continues in semiquavers.

sections.label: C · Con moto, rising line
sections.mNote: High notes, first soft, build to a forte passage.

sections.label: Coda · High sextuplets, two closing chords
sections.mNote: The figures rise to pppp in the top octave.

cues.title: Left-hand melody from bar 3
cues.text: The right hand begins alone, playing thirds at pp. Two bars later the left hand enters with the melody, marked mf, below the continuing right-hand thirds.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 1, bars 1–5: Moderato, two opening bars for right hand alone, left-hand melody from bar 3. https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/7-morceaux-de-salon-op-10/barcarolle-op-10-no-3.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Barcarolle in G minor, 1894
cues.text: In 1894 Rachmaninoff placed this G minor boat song third among his seven Morceaux de salon. The opening lies under both hands, played quietly. The quick passages later take the right hand high up the keyboard.
cues.evidence: Piano Street’s work entry dates Op. 10 No. 3 to 1894 and identifies its place in the seven Morceaux de salon; the score shows the opening and the later high piano writing. https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/7-morceaux-de-salon-op-10/barcarolle-op-10-no-3.htm

cues.title: Con moto section
cues.text: At Con moto the right hand changes to running semiquavers, marked ppp leggiero, very quiet and light. The left hand moves up into the treble clef and holds its chords while the right-hand figures continue above.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 3, final two systems: Con moto, ppp, leggiero and tied left-hand chords in treble clef.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the left-hand melody
cues.text: The left-hand melody returns at Allegro moderato, again marked mf, and keeps its broad pace. Above it, the right hand has more notes than at the opening and fills the rocking pattern with ppp semiquavers.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 6: Allegro moderato, mf left-hand melody and ppp semiquaver accompaniment.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Edison recording, 1919
cues.text: Rachmaninoff recorded the Barcarolle for Edison in April 1919. The disc, Diamond Disc 82202, was issued in February 1921, with Chopin’s Waltz in A♭, Op. 64 No. 3, on the other side.
cues.evidence: Richard Densmore’s Edison Diamond Disc list: 82202, released 2/1921, with the Barcarolle (matrix 6743) on one side and Chopin’s Valse in A♭, Op. 64 No. 3 (matrix 6736) on the other, both recorded in April 1919: https://www.densmore-edisondd.info/EdisonRecordsList/index.html . The Discography of American Historical Recordings catalogues the disc and its two matrices: https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/234970

cues.title: Closing bars, top octave
cues.text: The quick figures make a diminuendo and rise into the top octave, marked pppp. The bass stops while the last sextuplets climb. Two separate chords close the piece, ppp and then pp.
cues.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 10: diminuendo, pppp sextuplets with 8va, then two closing chords marked ppp and pp.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The left hand holds its chord
transitions.to: B · Semiquavers and held chords, ppp
transitions.how: At Con moto, the right hand changes from thirds to continuous semiquavers, marked ppp leggiero. The left hand gives up its melody, moves into the treble clef and holds a chord tied across the bar line, below the right-hand semiquavers.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 3, final two systems: Con moto, leggiero, semiquavers and tied left-hand chord.

transitions.title: Left-hand melody returns at Allegro moderato
transitions.from: B · Semiquavers and held chords, ppp
transitions.to: A′ · Low melody again, Allegro moderato
transitions.how: The quick right-hand writing makes a crescendo to f, then a diminuendo to pp. At Allegro moderato, Rachmaninoff brings back the left-hand tune at mf, below right-hand semiquavers marked ppp.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 6: crescendo to f, diminuendo, pp and Allegro moderato.

transitions.title: Diminuendo to ppp and Meno mosso
transitions.from: A′ · Low melody again, Allegro moderato
transitions.to: A″ · Slower figures over held chords
transitions.how: The returning melody makes a diminuendo through pp to ppp. At Meno mosso the right-hand semiquavers slow, and the left hand holds a low chord tied across the bar line. The rocking figure continues at the slower tempo.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 8: diminuendo, pp, ppp and Meno mosso with a tied bass chord.

transitions.title: The right hand climbs again
transitions.from: A″ · Slower figures over held chords
transitions.how: The right hand climbs from ppp under the marking Con moto. The left hand rests briefly, then holds chords in the treble clef. The semiquavers climb, the chords begin to move, and a crescendo takes both hands to f.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 9: Con moto, ppp, held treble-clef chords and crescendo to f.

transitions.title: Sextuplets rise to the high octave
transitions.to: Coda · High sextuplets, two closing chords
transitions.how: The right-hand semiquavers descend over held left-hand chords, with a diminuendo. The bass then stops, and rising sextuplets take the hands into the high octave at pppp. Two closing chords, marked ppp and pp, end the piece.
transitions.evidence: Piano Street score, p. 10: diminuendo, pppp sextuplets, 8va and the two final chords.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Solo piano, performed by the composer
fields.note: No performing score edition is identified, and the printed text is not asserted to match the performance.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Sources agree on April 1919 and disagree on the day. The Archive filenames, the RCA register and the Library of Congress bulletin give 23 April; DAHR’s Edison ledger entry and the Classical Pianists chronology give 24 April. The day is not resolved here.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives New York for every take. The Library of Congress bulletin names Edison Studios, New York. The label place of publication, Orange, New Jersey, is not the session place.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Edison is the original label (released at Orange, New Jersey, according to DAHR’s label record); the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Edison Diamond Disc 82202 (10-inch double-faced; Barcarolle on side L, Chopin’s Valse in A♭, Op. 64 No. 3, on side R); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
fields.note: The side assignment and disc number are documented by the Edison list and the Library of Congress bulletin; the disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified. DAHR’s MARC record for the disc gives 10-inch, 80 rpm and a bracketed publication year of [1919], which predates the release documented by Densmore (February 1921) and by the Library of Congress ([1921]) and is not followed for the release date; either year is before 1926.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The RCA register names Edison 6743-C for CD 10, track 16, and the Archive file is that track. Edison issued all three takes (A, B, C) on the same catalogue number, so the disc number alone does not identify the take, and no comparison of takes was made. DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
fields.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Edison Diamond Disc 82202, released February 1921).
fields.note: Densmore’s Edison list gives a February 1921 release for 82202, and the Library of Congress Cataloging Service Bulletin 61 catalogues the disc as Edison [1921]; this is independent of the April 1919 session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

dossier.credit: Sergei Rachmaninoff, piano — Barcarolle, Op. 10 No. 3. Edison Diamond Disc 82202-L, matrix 6743 (New York, April 1919). Digital source: RCA/BMG Complete Recordings (1992), CD 10, via Internet Archive; Public Domain Mark 1.0 is the item’s licence statement.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
